name: Live Free or Die!™

pitch_detail.notes: Clean face climbing past several bolts and V2-V3-ish overlaps; mostly on-your-feet bolted climbing low on the East Face.
Continuation of bolted slab climbing past more overlaps in the same clean-face style as P1.
Easy-to-follow, mostly bolted face climbing to a bolted pedestal belay beneath a broad roof, just left of the Independence Route's quartz chimney.

The route's namesake crux: a sideways, height-dependent downclimb-dyno roughly partway up the pitch, crimpy and reachy, with bolt protection backing up the pendulum; finishes on excellent 5.10-5.11+ face climbing. Established via toprope over six weeks by Herrington, Hadley, and Keena-Levin in summer 2017.
Step right onto a mostly bolted pitch ending with a delicate V3 mantle to a tiny stance; protection mixes bolts, gear, and old pitons in the overlaps.
A height-dependent V4 move gains a flake, then a thin crack system takes small gear up to a nice ledge below a massive roof.
Climb left past a bolt through the roof, follow 5.9 cracks to a bolted leftward traverse, then back-clean the leftmost bolt on the way across.
Splitter hand cracks lead to M&M Ledge, the shared mid-height junction with Thin Red Line, where most parties either rappel or continue up Thin Red Line's finish to the summit.

rappel_detail.pull: A single 60 m rope reaches the ledge with room to spare. Knot both ends as a matter of habit.
rappel_detail.notes: Reached by downclimbing the upper pitch about 20 ft from the summit, then moving left (east). First of the three single-rope rappels.
hazards: These trees are the only marker for the top of the descent and are easy to walk past on the summit ridge; a party that misses them commits itself to downclimbing the loose east gully instead.
The lower tree's slings are periodically found tired. Carry cord or webbing to replace rather than rappelling on whatever happens to be there.
Snow can linger on the landing ledge into early season.
rappel_detail.station: Reverse the last pitch roughly 15-20 m (about 50 ft) from the summit and work toward the Concord Tower side of the crest. The anchor is a tree carrying fixed slings, tucked off the crest near a shallow groove in the rock; two slung trees stand close together and the upper one is the sounder of the pair. It is much easier to pick out while leading pitch 4 than from above, so note it on the way up. The rappel lands on a sandy, tree-dotted ledge.

rappel_detail.pull: A plumb pull off bolts. Keep the strands clear of the ledge lip and its trees so nothing catches on the retrieve.
rappel_detail.notes: Second station, on a large ledge reached by scrambling down and to the right from the first rappel.
hazards: Loose sand and grit on the ledge above slabby downclimbing.
If the chains are not found after the ropes are pulled, the party is stranded between stations with no anchor.
rappel_detail.station: Do not rappel straight on from the sandy ledge. Work right along the ledge, then down, then right again to reach a fixed station of bolts and chains on the steep wall. Parties consistently report this hardware as hard to spot, so scout it before pulling the first rope.

rappel_detail.pull: Because the rappel is diagonal, the pull strand drags across the wall and this descent has a documented history of jammed ropes. One party had to fix one strand, lead back up the climbable ground to free it, then ascend to the station and re-rig. Feed the pull strand out and away from the diagonal, and pull from the notch rather than from directly under the anchor.
rappel_detail.notes: Rappels somewhat diagonally into the Liberty Bell-Concord notch at about 7,300 ft. Downclimb the gully from there to the packs.
hazards: The line traverses, so anyone who loses the stance swings across the wall.
The notch and the gully below it are loose, and anything dislodged here funnels onto the climbers' path that other parties are walking up.
rappel_detail.station: The lowest fixed station on the wall, straight below the previous one. The rappel from it runs slightly diagonally rather than plumb and finishes in the Liberty Bell-Concord notch at roughly 7,300 ft, close to where most parties leave packs at the top of the approach gully.

rappels: 3 single-rope rappels with a 60 m rope on the standard Liberty Bell descent: one off slung trees just below the summit, then two of about 25 m from bolted anchors into the Liberty Bell-Concord notch. Downclimbing the first section instead leaves two.
descent_text: Live Free or Die climbs the East Face for 8 pitches to M&M Ledge (roughly mid-height), then shares its final 3-4 pitches to the summit with the upper section of Thin Red Line. Parties who finish on the summit take the standard Liberty Bell descent. From the summit, downclimb the upper pitch a short way and go left (east) to a tree hung with rappel slings. One single-rope rappel with a 60 m rope reaches a sandy ledge; work right and down to a bolted station, then make two single-rope rappels of about 25 m from bolted anchors into the Liberty Bell-Concord notch at about 7,300 ft. Parties who downclimb the ridge and the 5.6 boulder problem to the first bolts instead of making the tree rappel do two rappels in all. From the notch, downclimb the loose gully back to the climbers’ path and the Blue Lake Trail. Parties who stop at M&M Ledge can instead take Thin Red Line’s rappel line: from M&M Ledge, rappel with two ropes off a fixed pin and wire, then work climber’s left to bolted anchors and make four more double-rope rappels to the talus at the base of the East Face.
approach: Same East Face approach as Liberty Crack: park at the hairpin turn on WA-20 east of Washington Pass, walk back to the pond on the south side of the road, and follow the cairned climbers' path from the pond's east end about a mile through forest to the talus below the East Face. The route begins in the same general area as Liberty Crack and the Independence Route on the lower East Face — verify you're at the correct start, since several route lines begin within a short distance of each other along the base talus.
overview: Despite its name and grade label, Live Free or Die! is NOT a boulder problem — it is a full 11-pitch, roughly 1,200-foot free route up Liberty Bell's East Face (grade 5.12- yds; crux may feel 5.12b for shorter climbers), sharing a few meters and belay stances with the Independence Route. Established in summer 2017 by Seth Keena-Levin, Nathan Hadley, and Blake Herrington. Mostly 5.10-5.11 thin face climbing leads to a reachy, bouldery crux sequence ending in a downclimb past two bolts.
beta: P1-3 (5.8-5.11) climb bolted overlaps; P4 (5.12, V5 crux) is height-dependent rightward crimping with an optional pendulum; P5 (5.11) is mostly bolted with a delicate V3 mantle finish; P6 (~5.11d) is a thin crack needing small gear; P7 (5.11+) roof climbing into a 5.10 slab traverse; P8 (5.10) a splitter hands crack to M&M Ledge; P9-11 follow Thin Red Line to the summit.
gear: quickdraws with a few finger-size cams for pitches 1-3 and 5
standard rack to 3 inches for pitches 4, 6, 7, and 8
fa: Blake Herrington, Nathan Hadley & Seth Keena-Levin, 2017
